title: Quantum algorithm for stochastic optimal stopping problems with applications in finance
abstract_summary: The paper proposes a quantum version of the least-squares Monte Carlo (LSM) algorithm to solve stochastic optimal stopping problems (notably American option pricing), combining quantum sampling access to the underlying process, quantum circuits that compute stopping times in superposition, and quantum Monte Carlo subroutines. Under mild smoothness assumptions on the continuation values the method attains a near-quadratic runtime speedup in the Monte Carlo error parameter compared to classical LSM; the authors provide detailed error and complexity analyses and case studies for Brownian and geometric Brownian motion models.
methodology_description: This is a theoretical / algorithmic study proposing a quantum analogue of the classical Least Squares Monte Carlo (LSM) algorithm for discrete-time stochastic optimal stopping problems (e.g., American option pricing). The authors define a quantum input model (quantum sampling access to a Markov chain and quantum query access to payoff and basis functions), a fixed-point arithmetic model, and access to controlled-rotation primitives. The quantum LSM replaces classical Monte Carlo estimation of necessary expectation values with quantum Monte Carlo subroutines (Montanaro-style amplitude-estimation-based mean estimation) to estimate matrix entries A_t = E[e_{t,k}(X_t) e_{t,l}(X_t)] and vectors b_t = E[Z_{tau_{t+1}} e_t(X_t)]. A central construction is a family of unitaries W_t and V^{(k)}_t that compute stopping times in superposition and produce controlled-access to the path-dependent payoff quantities Ze_{tau_t} e_{t-1,k}(x_{t-1}). Those unitaries are used inside the quantum Monte Carlo routines to obtain the entries of b_t and of the A_t matrices (or, in some special cases, exploit orthogonality to avoid estimating A_t). After quantum estimation of A_t and b_t entries, the algorithm forms eA_t and e b_t classically and computes e alpha_t = eA_t^{-1} e b_t (classical inversion). The dynamic programming / stopping-time recursion is performed backward from T to 0; at each stage the algorithm must re-prepare prior unitaries in superposition, so the quantum algorithm incurs an extra T factor compared to one-pass classical LSM. The paper performs a detailed error analysis that combines: (i) statistical / sampling error from quantum mean estimation, (ii) sensitivity analysis for solving the linear systems (bounds via condition / min singular value), and (iii) approximation error from projecting continuation values onto a finite-dimensional basis. To bound approximation errors the authors consider polynomial approximation spaces (Rq), apply Jackson-type inequalities under smoothness assumptions (C^n or Lipschitz), and analyze two canonical stochastic models (Brownian motion with Hermite polynomials and geometric Brownian motion with monomials/Vandermonde structure) to obtain explicit bounds and complexities. Complexity and probabilistic error bounds are derived, showing regimes where the quantum algorithm achieves near-quadratic speedup in the ǫ-dependence relative to the classical LSM under regularity assumptions. The work is wholly algorithmic and analytic; no empirical experiments are reported.

results_summary: This preprint presents a theoretical quantum algorithm that adapts the classical Least-Squares Monte Carlo (LSM) approach for stochastic optimal stopping (notably American option pricing) to a quantum computing setting. The core idea is to compute stopping times in quantum superposition and to use quantum Monte Carlo (amplitude-estimation style) subroutines to estimate continuation-value integrals, combined with projection onto finite-dimensional approximation spaces (polynomial bases). The authors derive detailed complexity and error bounds showing that, under assumptions (quantum sampling/query access to the process and functions, sufficient smoothness of continuation values, control of Gram-matrix conditioning), the quantum algorithm reduces the dependence on the Monte Carlo error parameter ε roughly from ε^{-2} (classical) to ε^{-1} (quantum), up to polylogarithmic and problem-dependent factors. They also analyze special cases (Brownian and geometric Brownian motion) and discuss caveats such as T^2 overhead in time-step recursion and strong dependence on approximation parameters and condition numbers. No experimental validation is provided.

quantum_advantage_detail: The paper provides theoretical complexity proofs showing a near-quadratic improvement in the dependence on the Monte Carlo error parameter ε (from ε^{-2} classically to ε^{-1} quantumly) under specific assumptions: availability of quantum sampling/query oracles, sufficiently smooth continuation values (polynomial approximation error small), and favorable conditioning of basis Gram matrices. No empirical demonstration is provided, and practical usefulness depends strongly on oracle construction costs, T^2 overhead, basis conditioning (σ_min), and dimensional/smoothness parameters.
limitations: Requires quantum sampling access to the Markov chain (oracle U) which can be hard to construct for continuous/real-world models (authors note Grover–Rudolph and discretization issues).

Assumes quantum query access to payoff and basis functions and a quantum arithmetic model that treats arithmetic operations (fixed-point arithmetic, controlled rotations, etc.) as constant-cost primitives — costs that are deferred and not accounted for in the runtime (authors).
Algorithm needs a known lower bound on the minimum singular value σ_min(At) of feature matrices At (authors); this affects variance bounds used in quantum Monte Carlo subroutines.
Quadratic quantum speedup is contingent on smoothness of continuation values (E[Z_{τ_{t+1}}|X_t] ∈ C^n) with n = Θ(log(1/ε)/log log(1/ε)) — a nontrivial regularity assumption (authors).

Complexities have very unfavorable dependence on number of time steps T (often T^2 or worse) and in many parameter regimes exponential dependence on q, d, or (5T/ε)^{const}, especially for geometric Brownian motion (authors).
Analysis uses finite-dimensional polynomial approximation spaces and Jackson-like bounds; approximation error terms depend implicitly on the underlying Markov chain and chosen basis (authors).
Assumes ability to evaluate/implement basis functions et,k efficiently in superposition (may be nontrivial for complex bases); cost Te is treated as a black-box (authors).
The algorithm recomputes the dynamic-programming steps repeatedly and works in superposition, yielding O(T^2) steps instead of O(T) (authors).
Error bounds and runtime hide many polylog and constant factors (authors).

key_ideas: #idea:quantum-advantage — Replaces classical Monte Carlo mean estimation in LSM with amplitude-estimation-style quantum mean estimation to obtain a near-quadratic speedup in the Monte Carlo error parameter (ε^{-2} → ~ε^{-1} up to polylog factors) under regularity assumptions.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Uses a hybrid workflow: quantum subroutines (state preparation, stopping-time unitaries, amplitude-estimation-based mean estimation) produce estimated matrix/vector entries, while matrix inversion and some postprocessing are performed classically.

#idea:quantum-advantage — Formal complexity bounds and error analyses are provided showing regimes where quantum LSM attains the claimed ε-dependence improvement; explicit scalings are derived for polynomial approximation spaces.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Central construction uses unitaries that compute stopping times in superposition and feed controlled-payoff registers into quantum mean estimation routines; classical inversion of estimated Gram matrices yields continuation coefficients.

#idea:quantum-advantage — Case studies for Brownian motion (Hermite basis) and geometric Brownian motion (monomial/Vandermonde basis) give concrete complexity bounds and demonstrate situations with better/worse dependencies.

#idea:hybrid-approach — The algorithm accrues additional overhead from re-preparing prior-time unitaries during the backward dynamic-programming recursion, introducing an extra factor in T (time steps) compared to classical LSM.

#idea:quantum-advantage — Detailed error decomposition: (i) quantum mean-estimation statistical error, (ii) sensitivity from linear-system solves (condition/min singular value dependence), and (iii) projection/approximation error from finite basis approximation.

#idea:hybrid-approach — The speedup claim crucially depends on access assumptions (quantum sampling/query access to the underlying Markov chain and payoff/basis functions) and smoothness/regularity of continuation values.
contradictions: contradiction:scalability — Although the algorithm attains a near-quadratic improvement in the ε-dependence under idealised assumptions, the paper shows that this advantage can be negated or heavily attenuated by problem-dependent factors (number of basis functions m, dimension d, smoothness n, condition numbers σ_min, norms of basis/payoff functions) and an extra T overhead from re-running unitaries; hence the asymptotic ε-speedup does not imply practical scalability to realistic, high-dimensional option pricing instances.

contradiction:scalability — The method requires strong quantum input models (quantum sampling / query access and efficient state preparation) which are non-trivial and potentially costly; without accounting for data-encoding/state-preparation costs the stated complexity advantage may be overly optimistic.
